questions.question: Just wondering, what is the best way to clean the wok after each use? And should I use the heat & coat in oil technique after each use as well?

hybrid.answer:
Kenji's routine after each use is to rinse, dry the wok on the burner, and rub in a very thin film of oil. The oil step matters most if you'll store the wok. If you cook in it daily, it matters much less. This is from his most recent wok AMA (March 2026), and his earlier videos agree.

**Cleaning**
- He recommends rinsing it right after cooking, and says soap is fine if you need it. [1][2]
- For anything stuck on, he says to rub with a scrubber. A bamboo wok brush is his favorite because it gives good leverage. [3][4]
- For really burnt-on food, he says to heat the wok, add water and scrub. He says that won't damage it. [5]

**Heat to dry**
- He puts the rinsed wok back on the burner. He says this is "not about seasoning" but about getting it dry, because wiping with a towel still leaves some moisture. [2][6]
- In his January 2026 video he cleans the new wok the same way: rinse, wipe out the oil, then heat it to dry. With the super nitride coating, he says you don't need to be as careful about drying as with cast iron, but it still helps maintain the seasoning. [7]

**Oil coat afterward**
- Once it's completely dry, he rubs in a final little layer of oil. [8]
- He says the oil is not that important if you use the wok every day or even several times a day. It is important if you store it somewhere with moisture in the air, because a raw carbon steel wok can rust. [9]
- He says it's "not too much of an issue" with his super nitrided wok, because it isn't reactive the way carbon steel is. [10]
- Keep the coat very thin. A thick layer can turn gummy over time, so he says to put some oil on and then wipe it out as if you'd accidentally put it there. [11][12]

**Seasoning**
- He says not to try to build up polymer or burnt-on carbon layers. He washes his wok smooth each time he cooks. [13]

questions.question: A genuine question: if a wok doesn't build up layers of polymers like a cast iron, what does it mean for a wok to build up seasoning?

hybrid.answer:
For Kenji, wok seasoning mostly means one thing: turning raw carbon steel into black oxide. After that it's a light, per-use upkeep, not a growing layer.

**The initial seasoning.** He says that with a wok "it's not about building up layers of polymers." It's about the initial step, converting the raw steel into black oxide [1]. You do that by heating the wok until the surface turns black or bluish black. On gas he says to heat it in different spots until the whole surface changes [2]. The first heating is what turns the silvery steel black, and he says that black oxide layer "could be considered seasoning" [3].

**Why polymers don't build up.** He gives two reasons:
- The bottom of a wok gets far hotter than the edges, so the metal warps and expands unevenly every time you cook. Hard polymer layers have a tough time sticking [4].
- You almost always deglaze with a liquid that is often acidic, which strips the seasoning [5].

He adds that you shouldn't expect or aim for thick polymer seasoning in a wok [3].

**What ongoing seasoning looks like.** He describes it as more of a per-use thing [3][6]. At home he starts by rubbing a little oil into the wok with a paper towel, about a quarter to half a teaspoon [7].

His view is consistent across the videos, from the 2022 wok-seasoning video through the 2026 wok AMA.

questions.question: Is there any advantage to salting hours ahead of time with this technique, or does the long time the steak spends hanging out in the oven make that moot? [reverse sear]

hybrid.answer:
Yes, by his account there is an advantage, though he doesn't speak to the oven-time question directly. In his reverse sear video he salts the steak and lets it rest before it goes in the oven. He says 45 minutes is the minimum and that overnight is an option.

**What he does with the reverse sear (2025)**
- He seasons heavily with salt, pepper and a little MSG, then lets the steak sit before cooking. He says salt first pulls moisture out, and the brine that forms then breaks down some muscle proteins and the steak reabsorbs the moisture [1][2].
- Because those proteins are broken down, they don't tighten as much when cooked, so less moisture gets squeezed out. He says you get a moister steak and "better more penetrative seasoning" [2].
- He sets the steak aside for about 45 minutes, which he calls about the minimum time for this to happen. If you prefer, you can leave it uncovered in the fridge overnight. The surface dries and forms a pellicle, so it sears even better, but he says 45 minutes is enough [2].

**His newer, related test (January 2026)**
This one is a pan-seared tenderloin, not a reverse sear. He compares a steak salted and left uncovered overnight with an unsalted one. He says the salted steak ends up juicier and more tender, browns a deeper mahogany, and its juices stay in rather than running out quickly [3][4][5]. He also says you can cook a great steak without salting ahead, and that it's partly a matter of preference [5][6].

**What he hasn't said**
In the material available here, he doesn't say whether the time in the low oven does the same job as salting ahead, or whether hours of salting before a reverse sear beat 45 minutes. What he does say is that 45 minutes is enough for the reverse sear, and that longer, uncovered, gives a drier surface for searing.

questions.question: So, Kenji, since you left Cook's Illustrated, they've started to advocate cold searing (starting in a cold pan and flipping every 2 minutes until done). What are your thoughts?

hybrid.answer:
Kenji hasn't covered cold-pan searing or flipping steak every couple of minutes in the videos available here, so there's no verdict from him on Cook's Illustrated's newer approach.

The closest thing he did say is that he still prefers the reverse sear he developed at Cook's Illustrated. In 2025 he called it "still my favorite way to cook a big steak" [1]. He says it gives a much more even cook from edge to center than the traditional sear-then-oven method, which gives a bullseye pattern [2].
